name: Sunbed + MT2 stack

lead: The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster and deeper. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions, with users reporting a deep tan in fewer sessions.

The chain is two-part: melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly, and proponents expect the two to add together. Each part is known to darken skin on its own; no studies have tested the combination.

paras: Users combine the peptide with regular sunbed sessions over several weeks, in the belief that melanin is already primed when UV arrives. Descriptions come from user reports rather than trials.

Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators have warned against it since 2007. UV tanning devices are classified by IARC as Group 1 carcinogens and are linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.

angle.text: You combine tanning-bed sessions with melanotan II to build a deep tan in fewer sessions than either alone: the peptide boosts melanin production and UV triggers pigment. Each part is known to darken skin by itself. The combination has not been trialled and rests on user reports.

lead: The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice that pairs indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed synthetic analogue of the hormone alpha-MSH, to build a deep tan faster than either would alone. Practitioners want darker, more even skin colour, which many in these communities say adds contrast, definition and a leaner, healthier-looking face and body [1][2][3][4].

Melanotan II stimulates melanin production through melanocortin receptors. Reported effects include darkening of moles and freckles, flushing, nausea, appetite reduction and, in men, erections. It has never been approved as a medicine, and unlicensed products are sold online, in some gyms and salons, and more recently on social media in nasal-spray form [1][5]. Indoor tanning devices emit mostly UVA with a little UVB, and improving appearance is the most commonly cited reason people tan indoors [2].

Health agencies have warned against unlicensed melanotan since 2007, and the World Health Organization classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that a 2021 review attributed the higher melanoma rates among melanotan users to their greater UV exposure rather than the peptide itself, while a 2013 review found no conclusive evidence that melanotan causes melanoma [1]. No clinical trial of the combination has been published.
infobox: Synthetic alpha-MSH analogue, unlicensed; non-selective melanocortin agonist [1]

paras: The stack is the combination of two separate practices. Melanotan II acts on melanocortin receptors to increase melanin and may increase sexual arousal through MC4 receptor activation [1]. Sunbeds darken existing melanin with UVA and, through their small UVB output, stimulate new melanin [2]. Users describe the pairing as a way to need fewer or shorter sunbed sessions, a belief that rests on community reports rather than trials [3].

The aim in looksmaxxing terms is appearance. Forum members ask whether a tan improves a man's looks or leaves him looking over-bronzed, and some describe a tan as the final step after grooming, hair, brow and skincare changes [3][4]. Writers on UK tanning culture have tied the growth of nasal-spray melanotan to influencer marketing and to a wider willingness among young people to accept risk for cosmetic results [5].

Scientists at the University of Arizona developed melanotan I and II in the 1980s as possible sunless tanning agents. One of the researchers reported a prolonged erection with nausea and vomiting after a self-administered dose, which is part of how the sexual effect was noticed [1]. Melanotan I (afamelanotide) was licensed to an Australian start-up that became Clinuvel, and the FDA approved afamelanotide in 2019 for a rare genetic sun sensitivity. Melanotan II was licensed to Palatin Technologies for sexual dysfunction research but never approved; Palatin stopped development in 2000 and moved to bremelanotide, which the FDA approved in 2019 [1].

Pharmacologically, melanotan II is a non-selective agonist of melanocortin receptors MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5. MC1 activation drives melanin production, MC4 activation is thought to underlie the sexual effects, and MC4 also contributes to reduced appetite [1]. Reported effects include reversible darkening of moles and freckles, facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning, stretching and loss of appetite [1].

Early small clinical trials of both melanotans found increased melanin, and one study suggested some protection from sunburn; Cancer Research UK described these as early-stage and unconfirmed and noted that a tan offers limited protection from UV [6].

Friedrich Wolff invented the sunbed in 1975, and salons spread across Europe and North America in the late 1970s [2]. Tanned skin had become fashionable decades earlier; the article on indoor tanning dates the shift to Coco Chanel's tan in 1923, and the Danish physician Niels Ryberg Finsen's UV lamp work of the 1890s earned a 1903 Nobel Prize for treating skin disease [2]. Modern beds emit no UVC, little UVB and mostly UVA. UVA gives a quick tan by darkening existing melanin; UVB triggers new melanin and a longer-lasting tan. Horizontal low-pressure beds typically run 15 to 20 minutes, high-pressure beds are shorter and emit more UVA, and high-pressure beds can deliver 10 to 15 times the UVA of midday sun [2].

Wikipedia lists improving appearance, including looking thinner and covering blemishes, as the most common reason for tanning indoors, alongside pre-holiday tans and mood benefits that users link to endorphins [2]. Some researchers argue moderate bed use can supply vitamin D, while most hold that the risks outweigh this and that supplements are safer [2].

No studies found on the combination of sunbeds and melanotan II. Studies of sunbeds alone are observational and meta-analytic. A 2012 BMJ systematic review of 27 observational studies found a summary relative risk of melanoma of 1.20 for ever-use of sunbeds, 1.25 in cohort and population studies, and a relative risk of 1.87 for first use before age 35 [7]. A 2019 review in Current Opinion in Oncology concluded that the epidemiological criteria for causality are met for sunbeds and melanoma [8]. A 2022 review described well-documented negative effects with no clear benefit beyond cosmetic outcomes [9]. An Icelandic data analysis cited in a 2022 review linked a rise in melanoma in young women to sunbed use, and reported that incidence fell after a campaign against sunbeds; the authors noted that young-adult melanoma mortality stayed very low [10]. A commentary on the earlier Icelandic study cautioned that its ecologic design limits interpretation [11].

A study of tanning induced by a sunbed-type treatment examined how induced pigmentation affects UV-induced DNA damage in human skin in situ [12]. Case reports describe sunbed-related lentigines and pseudoporphyria [13].

For melanotan II, Wikipedia cites a 2013 review finding no conclusive evidence that it causes melanoma, a 2021 review attributing higher melanoma rates among users to heavier UV exposure, and a 2020 mouse study in which it suppressed melanoma progression [1]. A British Medical Journal report described by Cancer Research UK covered two fair-skinned women who developed intense tans and rapidly changing moles after using sunbeds and injecting melanotan I and II bought online [6].

Agencies in Norway (December 2007), Denmark (2008), the UK (2008), Ireland (February 2009) and the FDA (a warning letter in January 2009) issued warnings about unlicensed melanotan products, citing legality, case reports and possible impurities [1]. In January 2009 the UK regulator MHRA said melanotan was advertised and sold illegally and said it had contacted 18 companies to stop supplying and advertising it; the FDA said that selling it violates federal law [6]. Cancer Research UK noted that illegally sold products leave buyers unable to know what they contain and that unsterile injecting can transmit infections [6].

A 2024 investigation by Moray Firth Radio reported nasal-spray melanotan II openly sold through hundreds of Instagram accounts, with TikTok videos of the spray drawing tens of millions of views. It reported that the MHRA regulates melanotan II as a medicine only in injectable form, that TikTok banned the #nasaltanning hashtag, and that experts and Cancer Research UK advised against use [5]. A Cancer Research UK spokesperson said the products have not been tested for safety, quality or effectiveness [5].

For sunbeds, Brazil banned cosmetic use in 2009 and Australia banned commercial tanning in 2015. France banned minors in 1997, and about 20 US states ban use by minors under 18; the FDA requires a boxed warning against use by under-18s [2]. A national survey of German tanning studios examined the advice staff gave after the country's 2012 UV regulation [14].

For UV tanning, the WHO's cancer agency classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, and a 2020 review recommends that prevention advice include avoiding sunbeds [15]. Indoor tanning is linked to basal cell, squamous cell and melanoma skin cancers, premature skin ageing, burns and eye damage [2][9]. Wikipedia also notes that tanning beds can harbour bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus [2].

For melanotan II, reported effects include nausea, vomiting, flushing, headaches, dizziness, skin and nail discolouration and changes to moles; the 2024 investigation also cited reports of kidney problems and a serious muscle-breakdown condition [1][5]. Cancer Research UK has warned that rapidly changing moles in users could complicate checks for skin cancer [6].
Excessive tanning has also been discussed as a psychiatric concern, sometimes called tanorexia, linked in studies to anxiety, eating disorders and smoking [2].

On looksmax.org, tanning is debated as an appearance tool. One thread asks whether sunbed tanning improves a man's looks or risks an over-tanned look; replies range from praise of the short-term effect to the view that it suits women better than men [3]. Another poster describes a weekly high-intensity sunbed session as the last item on a list that included hair, brow and beard changes, and expects muscle and hormone benefits [4]. A thread titled after a user's report of skin cancer after a first-ever session drew replies suggesting supplements such as beta carotene [16].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sunbed use is debated as a way to improve looks, with posters weighing short-term appearance against cancer risk; melanotan appears in wider tanning discussion and media coverage [3][16][4][5].
